title: The trap Builtin
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of The trap Builtin and identify at least two relevant syllabus points.
Apply the trap builtin in a small Bash example and verify the expected output or status.
Identify one edge case or failure mode and state how to test it safely.

content.intro: `trap` registers a handler for selected signals or shell events such as EXIT.
content.why_it_matters: The trap Builtin matters because reliable shell automation depends on making this behavior explicit, testing its boundaries, and documenting environment assumptions.

content_blocks.title: Concept flow: The trap Builtin
content_blocks.alt_text: Four-step concept flow for lesson 100: The trap Builtin. Steps: Register a trap; Run work; Exit or receive signal; Clean up without hiding status.
content_blocks.caption: Lesson-specific flow: Register a trap → Run work → Exit or receive signal → Clean up without hiding status.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: `trap` registers shell commands to handle selected signals or shell events. Cleanup handlers should be small and predictable, should not hide the original failure, and cannot catch every possible termination event.

items.title: Registering signal handlers
items.text: Observe process completion and its status; define what should happen on normal exit, command failure, and interruption.

items.title: Handling script exit
items.text: Define what “Handling script exit” means in this lesson, show it with a minimal example, and verify the expected result plus one limitation or edge case.

items.title: Cleanup functions
items.text: Call the function with normal and invalid inputs; inspect its printed data separately from its exit status and local state.

items.title: Preserving exit statuses during cleanup
items.text: Run a successful and a failing command, capture the status immediately, and show how the calling script responds.

items.title: Avoiding unexpected behavior in subshells
items.text: Define what “Avoiding unexpected behavior in subshells” means in this lesson, show it with a minimal example, and verify the expected result plus one limitation or edge case.

content_blocks.title: How it fits into Bash
content_blocks.text: `trap` registers a handler for selected signals or shell events such as EXIT. Keep cleanup idempotent, avoid masking the original failure status, and test normal exit, error exit, and interruption in a disposable environment.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Save the snippet in a temporary practice file and run it with the locally installed Bash interpreter. The CodeLeaf in-page preview displays reference output only; it does not execute Bash code. Some examples require commands already installed on your machine.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Discard the temporary file or reset the editor to the original snippet. The examples are designed not to modify important data.

content_blocks.title: Watch out
content_blocks.text: Start with independent harmless tasks, bound concurrency, record each result, and plan cleanup for both normal exit and interruption. Do not assume the same command options or newer Bash features exist on every operating system.

content_blocks.title: Check your result
content_blocks.text: Compare the observed output and exit status with the reference behavior. Change one input at a time, include a boundary or invalid input, and note what differs on your target Bash/utility version.

content_blocks.title: Version and safety note
content_blocks.text: Use a local test directory, avoid secrets in commands/history/logs, and check the installed interpreter with `bash --version`. This course remains draft until technical examples and assessments receive subject-matter review.

content.task: Build a small local example for “The trap Builtin” using synthetic input or a disposable practice directory. Explain what the command should do, check its output and exit status, and test one boundary or failure case.

hints: Reduce the problem to one command or one small function first.

content.expected_output: A documented example for “The trap Builtin” with the observed output/status, one tested boundary case, and an explicit statement of any version or utility dependency.
troubleshooting: If the snippet uses an external command, check availability with `command -v NAME` and consult that program’s local help.
If behavior differs by operating system or Bash version, record `bash --version` and check the official manual linked below.
For syntax-only validation run `bash -n script.sh`; this parses but does not execute the script.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a successful-looking output means the command succeeded.
common_mistakes.why: Output and exit status are separate signals, and a later command may replace `$?`.
common_mistakes.fix: Capture important statuses immediately and check all relevant pipeline stages.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying example commands straight into a production path.
common_mistakes.why: Real paths, permissions, input names, and external utility versions differ.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a disposable fixture and inspect the planned side effects first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating Bash-specific syntax as portable `sh` syntax.
common_mistakes.why: Arrays, `[[ ... ]]`, process substitution, and some parameter operators are extensions.
common_mistakes.fix: Name the interpreter and test the minimum supported version.

summary: The trap Builtin has specific syntax and behavior; verify it rather than relying on guesswork.
Preserve argument boundaries and keep shell commands separate from untrusted data.
